name: Question 15
problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)-2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ of the system's matrix $A$ is $v=[1,\text{ }1]^{T}.$ The vector $w={[\frac{1}{2},0]}^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$  Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

*Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.*
worked_solution:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =0,\,v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t+\frac{1}{2} \\ t\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that ${x}_{E}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are equilibrium solutions of the system since ${x}_{E}^{′}(t)=0.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/58564c40fcde276fb69732ce5926b7e350fe8963b51b21df0ce4de39e8481514.png)

Now, we consider some general solutions of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t+\frac{1}{2} \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

For example:

- When ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=t+\frac{3}{2} \\ y=t+1\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add it to the phase space:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/d03f88d2eab48a0557f05311cd0d13d956b2af954277d322fabc4091f3aef2d4.png)

- When ${c}_{1}=-1$ and ${c}_{2}=-1,$ we get the following curve: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-t-\frac{3}{2} \\ y=-t-1\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add it to the phase space:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/e0748b246241a44132c526d1419d301ec67579c1d1cfbac0854c8bfccea67dff.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/66a32254dcc579eb248d8691d0c079815e29b59c650fc4b38eaa47bfb1525ddc.png)
